Alex.confusing: How hugs and confusion interact with claimed visits. It was hard to tell which reports could be trusted when a Floofer or Kookaburra was in play.
Alex.fun: Round 2, when my Eagle visit gave real information and the table agreed on Finley fast. It was satisfying to see the claims line up, even though Finley turned out to be Farm.
Alex.change: Make the scoring less swingy. Banked stakes and the 5-point round bonus let a few big rounds decide everything, and I finished with 0 in my score pile.
Alex.regret: In round 1 I winked Drew, which pulled attention onto me, and the whole table then threw at me. In round 2 I threw 3 big cards (C12, C8, D6) on a read that turned out wrong. I would have kept the high cards and thrown low ones.

Blair.confusing: How the Meowfia stake bonus worked: it was announced as doubling, but the "Grudge" extra and the final bonus tallies weren't explained clearly.
Blair.fun: Round 3 as Mouser: I steered the table onto Ellis, a Farm player, and my 13 and 8 banked at double value.
Blair.change: Show how the final bonus is calculated, and make it easier to tell whether a claim is a lie or a confusion effect.
Blair.regret: In round 2 I threw both 7s at Finley after a single hug result, on the idea that only a Floofer would hug me. I should have noticed the hug could have come from a visitor and kept the 7s, or thrown just one.

Casey.confusing: How the Kookaburra's confusion and hugs interact with other reports, since a hug or confusion could make a truthful claim look false.
Casey.fun: Round 2 as the Mouser, claiming Turkey and steering the table to throw at Finley while my partner Ellis stayed safe, and the double-banked stake paid off.
Casey.change: Give Farm players a bit more verifiable information, since a single lying cat's claim can sway the whole table when nothing can be cross-checked.
Casey.regret: In round 3 I threw 3 high cards (H11, C9, D5) on Ellis. The only evidence was Alex's hug claim, and I never considered that Alex or Drew might be lying. I should have thrown 1 low card or kept my cards.

Drew.confusing: How Kookaburra confusion interacts with other roles' reports, since I couldn't tell which of my information to trust, and how hugs and visits get reported to others.
Drew.fun: Round 1, when my Tit guess on Alex hit and the whole table threw at him. Banking 33 points on one throw felt great.
Drew.change: Let the Storyteller confirm whether a claimed visit actually happened, or give dead or confused players a bit more information. Several rounds turned on unverifiable claims.
Drew.regret: In round 2 I accused Finley too early, then flipped, then threw at him on the table's consensus. I should have kept my Owl result and suspected Casey and Ellis as the real cats, since they had the most convenient stories. In round 3 I also staked 20 points on the consensus, when I should have kept the cards.

Ellis.confusing: How the Kookaburra's confusion and the Owl's no-visitor egg interacted. My Owl visit to Drew laid an egg on him, yet Drew was -1, which was hard to reconcile.
Ellis.fun: Round 1, when the Eagle visit caught the Drew and Alex contradiction and the table converged on the Mouser. Round 2, the Kookaburra bluff that got Finley eggsecuted, was fun too.
Ellis.change: Give the table some way to verify claims, or limit how fast a CAW pile-on can end the day. A lone Farm player with a true report has little chance once the others agree.
Ellis.regret: In round 3 I accused Alex and Finley and claimed Owl, but I should have first asked Casey and Drew precisely who visited whom. I also staked 2 cards at Finley, though I was probably going to be eggsecuted, so I should have kept them.

Finley.confusing: The "Grudge" doubling bonus that appeared in the round 3 result wasn't in the rules I was given, and the final score breakdown (bonus 25) wasn't clear either. I also couldn't tell whether a hugged player's visit still counted for Owl and Eagle reports.
Finley.fun: Round 2, when I worked out Ellis was the Floofer from the hug pattern while five players threw at me. Round 3, when I joined the Ellis consensus as a hidden cat, was also fun.
Finley.change: I'd make dawn reports say a little more, for example whether a hug happened, so players can't so easily make claims that contradict each other. I'd also tell players how many cards each score pile holds.
Finley.regret: In round 1, I pushed suspicion onto Drew too hard, and Drew was then winked. I'd have kept quiet or deflected more gently. In round 2 I staked three high cards while the table was voting me out, and I'd have staked less.

review.title: Stake Bank Heist
review.headline: Meowfia lost one round, then won two by framing Farm players.
review.summary: Round 1 was a quick Farm win. Alex winked Drew mid-day, which confirmed a Mouser and the table piled onto Alex. In rounds 2 and 3 the table agreed on one Farm player each time and eggsecuted him, and the cats won both. Finley won with 80 points, mostly from banked stakes. Alex ended with 5 after losing every round.

rounds.recap: Alex (Mouser) winked Drew, who had just accused him. Drew was a Tit who had hit Mouser, so the wink exposed Alex. Everyone but Finley threw at Alex and he was eggsecuted. Farm won, and Drew banked 33 points on a heavy stake.

Finley (Hawk) was hugged and said so, but Owl Drew and Eagle Alex saw no Floofer visit him. The Floofer Ellis never visited him, so the table read his true claim as a lie. Finley was eggsecuted and the cats won. Finley still banked 32 by throwing at the real Floofer.

Ellis, a true Owl, contradicted Finley's fake Falcon claim. But Alex's hug and Casey's Eagle result both pointed at Ellis, who was Farm. The table, with Blair and Finley steering as cats, eggsecuted Ellis. Meowfia won and Finley and Blair banked 40 and 42.

highlights.text: Alex winks Drew right after Drew names him Mouser, which hands the table the proof it needs.
Finley tells the truth about being hugged and is eggsecuted for it, while the real Floofer helps the pile-on.
Ellis, a true Owl, correctly calls Finley a liar and is still eggsecuted by a Farm-heavy mob.
Finley and Blair, both cats, join the Ellis consensus and bank 80 and 67 points between them.

confusions.what: Said a hug claim was impossible, then reversed himself. He had misread that a Floofer hug does not need to show up in the Owl's visitor list.
Claimed Kookaburra is confused by any visitor, which is true, but his own report showed no confusion and nobody else's report was tested against it. He used a lie about his role as proof.
Treated a hugged Tit as evidence that Ellis was the Floofer. The Floofer was Finley, who visited Alex.
Read the Eagle result as proof Ellis hugged Alex, though it only shows who visited Ellis.
Claimed Hawk and said no egg meant Alex was not Meowfia. A hugged Alex would also give no egg, so the claim proved nothing.

worked: Throw counts and stakes: heavy stakes in round 1 gave big payoffs and made confidence visible.
Eagle and Owl visitor lists gave real cross-checks, which made the round 2 and 3 contradictions checkable.
The Mouser wink created a real moment in round 1, and it also backfired in an interesting way.
The hug effect made true claims look false, which gave Meowfia a real bluffing tool.
problems: Majority-Farm tables pile on whoever looks shakiest, and a Farm player was eggsecuted in both later rounds. Meowfia win easily because the 5 points plus 2x banking reward joining the mob. Consider a smaller reward for a Farm eggsecution.

Scores snowballed: Casey had 68 after round 2 and Finley's round 3 haul of 40 settled the game. Banked stakes are too large compared with the 5-point win bonus. Consider capping the stake or banking at face value.
Alex, Drew and others made random visits with no reasoning, so Night actions rarely produced useful information. A less random night or more informative roles would help.

The Hug is too strong and unclear: it makes true Farm claims read as lies, and the no-effect hug message tells the victim little. Let a hugged player learn they were hugged without a cover story, or add a way to verify.
The CAW CAW rule ends days after beat 2 or 3 every time. Discussion is short and the table agrees quickly. Consider needing four callers.
